title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
A ticket-routing review

A service desk checks whether an LLM routes tickets to the appropriate teams. A reviewer supplies reference decisions; the model supplies classifications. What would it mean for them to agree?

We will compare the reviewer reference outcome with the model classification ticket by ticket. The example is hypothetical. The reviewer decisions are operational references, not claims of error-free ground truth.

Introduce the task and the two sources of labels before displaying the table.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Which rows agree?

Mark exact agreement between the reviewer reference and model classification. How many of the six records agree?

Exact agreements occur on t2,t3,t5,t6t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6. Thus the observed agreement fraction is 4/6=2/34/6=2/3.

Ask for reasons on t1 and t4; do not yet call the fraction a future performance probability.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: What does four out of six describe?
text:
What does four out of six describe?

The table records four agreements. Is 4/64/6 a probability for every question about this model?

It is first an observed proportion in these six records. It becomes the probability of agreement if the experiment is to select one of these six ticket IDs uniformly. A claim about future tickets needs a target population and assumptions linking this audit to it.

Distinguish a data summary from a probability statement by asking for the experiment.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Equal-likelihood counting

If one of the six ticket IDs is selected uniformly, what is the probability that the selected record shows agreement?

The classical rule for a finite set of equally likely cases is P(E)=|E|/|Ω|P(E)=|E|/|\Omega|. Here each ID has probability 1/61/6 and four IDs show agreement, so P(agreement)=4/6=2/3P(\text{agreement})=4/6=2/3. The uniform selection rule justifies equal weights for IDs in this experiment.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
The cases being counted matter

The occupied reviewer/model pairs are: both destinations / Billing (t1t_1); Billing only / Billing (t2,t5t_2,t_5); Account only / Account (t3,t6t_3,t_6); Other / Account (t4t_4). If one pair type were selected uniformly, what agreement probability would result?

Two of four occupied types are agreements, so the answer under uniform selection among types is 2/4=1/22/4=1/2. It differs from 4/64/6 under uniform selection among ticket IDs because the categories contain unequal numbers of records.

Have students explain why changing the partition changes the sample unit and hence the selection rule.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: A larger set of possible label pairs
text:
A larger set of possible label pairs

There are four possible reviewer types and four model outputs (neither, Billing only, Account Support only, both). How many pairs are possible in their full Cartesian product? How many appear here?

There are 4×4=164\times4=16 possible pairs in the full product. Four are occupied in this six-row table. Uniform weighting over 16 pairs would give 4/16=1/44/16=1/4 agreement. This third selection rule is not implied by the audit.

Separate the set of possible combinations from the subset observed in the audit.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Frequency and repeated observations

Does an agreement fraction of 4/64/6 establish a long-run agreement rate for future tickets?

No. A frequency account connects probability to relative frequency in a specified repeatable process. If IiI_i indicates agreement on trial ii, the observed frequency after nn trials is n−1∑i=1nIin^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n I_i; a limiting account relates this sequence to a probability pp. Six observations alone establish no such limit and do not establish that future tickets follow the same process.

Keep observed frequency, model probability and future estimation distinct.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Belief and evidence

Suppose an analyst assigns probability 0.8 to agreement on the next ticket, given this audit and other information. Does the table alone determine 0.8?

No. A subjective account treats probability as a degree of belief given information. The assignment needs stated information or judgments and must be coherent with the analyst’s other probability assignments. An evidential account also needs a specified rule connecting evidence and background assumptions to a number.

State that these are interpretations, not competing arithmetic rules for the same fully specified experiment.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
What the earlier views contribute

What does each account emphasize: equal-likelihood counting, frequency, belief, or evidential support? What remains necessary for a calculation?

The accounts emphasize symmetry, repeated observations, information-conditioned belief, and evidential support. A calculation still needs specified outcomes, an event and a probability assignment. A propensity interpretation instead locates chance in a specified physical or randomized mechanism.

Use the slide as a transition, not a verdict on philosophical interpretations.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: A second question: a random chord
text:
A second question: a random chord

A chord is selected at random from a circle. What is the probability that its length exceeds the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle?

The phrase “at random” does not say how the chord is generated. Bertrand’s chord problem has answers 1/31/3, 1/21/2 and 1/41/4 under different sampling procedures. We will pose the question here and return to its full resolution in the supplement.

Show the chord illustration if space permits. Do not derive or choose a sampling procedure in the main lecture.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: What must a probability model specify?
text:
What must a probability model specify?

The ticket audit and the chord question both involve uncertainty. What mathematical objects would let us state the outcomes, the event and its probability?

Kolmogorov’s set-based framework specifies a sample space Ω\Omega, an event collection ℱ\mathcal F, and a probability measure PP. We now build these objects from the ticket-selection experiment.

Introduce the triplet only after students have named what is missing.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Specify the ticket experiment

The six records are fixed. We select one ticket ID uniformly. What varies, and what are the possible outcomes?

The selected ID varies. The sample space is Ω={t1,t2,t3,t4,t5,t6}\Omega=\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6\}. The ticket contents and labels are fixed data in this experiment.

Emphasize that the outcome is one ID, not a label or a probability.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Build the Billing event

Which ticket IDs have Billing in the reviewer’s reference outcome? Write them as a set BB.

B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}. An event is a set of outcomes in the sample space. The statement “Billing is required” occurs exactly when the selected ID belongs to BB.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Build the Account Support event

Which IDs have Account Support in the reviewer’s reference outcome? Write this event as AA.

A={t1,t3,t6}A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\}. The two events overlap because t1t_1 requires both destinations.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Other as a complement

In this two-destination question, “Other” means neither Billing nor Account Support is required. Express this event using AA and BB.

O=(B∪A)c={t4}O=(B\cup A)^c=\{t_4\}. The complement is taken relative to Ω\Omega. It does not mean the ticket is unreviewed or unknown; another team may handle it.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Union and intersection

Use the ticket IDs to find B∩AB\cap A and B∪AB\cup A. Interpret each event in words.

B∩A={t1}B\cap A=\{t_1\} means both destinations are required. B∪A={t1,t2,t3,t5,t6}B\cup A=\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\} means at least one is required. “Or” in a union is inclusive.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Count the union without double-counting

Why is the number of IDs in B∪AB\cup A not |B|+|A||B|+|A|? Calculate the probability under uniform selection.

The shared ID t1t_1 appears in both marginal counts. Split the union into disjoint parts: B\A={t2,t5}B\setminus A=\{t_2,t_5\}, A\B={t3,t6}A\setminus B=\{t_3,t_6\}, and B∩A={t1}B\cap A=\{t_1\}. Hence P(B∪A)=(2+2+1)/6=5/6P(B\cup A)=(2+2+1)/6=5/6. Equivalently, 3/6+3/6−1/6=5/63/6+3/6-1/6=5/6.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Pause and check the events

Without looking back, list the IDs in BB, AA, B∩AB\cap A, B∪AB\cup A and OO. Explain the overlap.

B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}; A={t1,t3,t6}A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\}; B∩A={t1}B\cap A=\{t_1\}; B∪A={t1,t2,t3,t5,t6}B\cup A=\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}; and O={t4}O=\{t_4\}. t1t_1 requires both named destinations.

Stop here if students need more practice with sets before formal requirements.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
The probability-space triplet

For uniform selection from the six ticket IDs, specify the sample space, the events and the probability assignment.

(Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)
Ω={t1,t2,t3,t4,t5,t6}\Omega=\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6\}.
ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega, the collection of all subsets of Ω\Omega.
For every E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F, P(E)=|E|/6P(E)=|E|/6.
Thus P(B)=3/6=1/2P(B)=3/6=1/2 and P(B∪A)=5/6P(B\cup A)=5/6.

First name each object, then write the symbols. Stress that the probability assignment depends on the stated uniform selection rule.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Outcomes, events and probability values

Classify each object: t2t_2, BB, and P(B)=1/2P(B)=1/2. Which one is the outcome? Which is an event? Which is a number?

t2t_2 is an outcome in Ω\Omega. BB is an event, a subset of Ω\Omega. P(B)=1/2P(B)=1/2 is a number assigned to that event. The measure takes events as input.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Requirements on the event collection

If EE is an event, should “not EE” also be an event? If E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots are events, what about “at least one occurs”?

A sigma-algebra ℱ\mathcal F on Ω\Omega satisfies:

Ω∈ℱ\Omega\in\mathcal F.
If E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F, then Ec∈ℱE^c\in\mathcal F.
If E1,E2,…∈ℱE_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F, then ⋃n=1∞En∈ℱ\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\mathcal F.

It therefore contains ⌀\varnothing too. In the finite ticket model, ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega satisfies these conditions.

These are closure requirements on the collection of events. Keep them distinct from the probability axioms on the next slide.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
A dashboard with limited information

A dashboard reports only Billing required or not. It distinguishes B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\} and Bc={t3,t4,t6}B^c=\{t_3,t_4,t_6\}. Which events can it represent?

𝒢={⌀,B,Bc,Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\} is a sigma-algebra. Its uniform-ID probabilities are 0,1/2,1/2,10,1/2,1/2,1. The subset {t1}\{t_1\} is unavailable in 𝒢\mathcal G. The full audit model uses 2Ω2^\Omega, which also distinguishes individual IDs.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Kolmogorov’s probability axioms

What conditions should a probability assignment satisfy on events?

For P:ℱ→[0,1]P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]:

Nonnegativity: P(E)≥0P(E)\ge0 for every E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F.
Normalization: P(Ω)=1P(\Omega)=1.
Countable additivity: for pairwise disjoint E1,E2,…∈ℱE_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F, P(⋃n=1∞En)=∑n=1∞P(En)P(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(E_n).

For example, BB and BcB^c are disjoint and exhaustive, and P(B)+P(Bc)=3/6+3/6=1P(B)+P(B^c)=3/6+3/6=1.

State nonnegativity, normalization and countable additivity separately from sigma-algebra closure.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
A random variable for Billing

Can we record numerically whether Billing is required? Define XBX_B on the ticket outcomes.

XB:Ω→ℝX_B:\Omega\to\mathbb R, where XB(t)=1X_B(t)=1 if t∈Bt\in B and XB(t)=0X_B(t)=0 if t∉Bt\notin B. The values are 1,1,0,0,1,01,1,0,0,1,0 on t1,…,t6t_1,\ldots,t_6 respectively. A random variable is a measurable function on outcomes; its inputs are individual outcomes. The probability measure is a set function on events. We will state measurability using inverse images. The selected outcome is random; for a given outcome, the function value is fixed.

Reinforce: the selected ticket outcome is random; the random variable is a function, not a second random mechanism.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: Image of a set of outcomes
text:
Image of a set of outcomes

For A={t1,t3,t6}A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\}, what values does XBX_B produce? Write the image XB(A)X_B(A).

XB(A)={XB(t):t∈A}={0,1}X_B(A)=\{X_B(t):t\in A\}=\{0,1\}. The image is a set of real values, not a set of ticket IDs.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Inverse image and probability

Which outcomes produce the value 1? Express them as XB−1({1})X_B^{-1}(\{1\}) and calculate P(XB=1)P(X_B=1).

XB−1({1})={t∈Ω:XB(t)=1}=B={t1,t2,t5}X_B^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t\in\Omega:X_B(t)=1\}=B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}. Therefore P(XB=1)=P(B)=3/6=1/2P(X_B=1)=P(B)=3/6=1/2. The inverse image is an event; it need not be an inverse function.

Trace the mapping in order: numerical condition, inverse-image event, probability of event.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: When a function is a random variable
text:
When a function is a random variable

To calculate P(XB∈D)P(X_B\in D), what must be true of XB−1(D)X_B^{-1}(D)? For D=(1/2,3/2)D=(1/2,3/2), identify that inverse image.

The inverse image is BB, an event. Formally, X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R is measurable if X−1(D)∈ℱX^{-1}(D)\in\mathcal F for every Borel set DD. Borel sets form the smallest sigma-algebra containing the open intervals; they include singletons and countable combinations of intervals.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: The law of the Billing indicator
text:
The law of the Billing indicator

The Billing indicator is 1 on t1,t2,t5t_1,t_2,t_5 and 0 otherwise. Under uniform ID selection, what probability law does it induce?

The law is PX(D)=P(X−1(D))P_X(D)=P(X^{-1}(D)). Here PXB({1})=1/2P_{X_B}(\{1\})=1/2 and PXB({0})=1/2P_{X_B}(\{0\})=1/2. Every inverse image is one of ⌀,B,Bc,Ω\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega, so XBX_B is measurable even for the smaller dashboard collection 𝒢\mathcal G.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: One die: outcome, event, value, probability
text:
One die: outcome, event, value, probability

Roll a stipulated fair die. Let Ωd={1,…,6}\Omega_d=\{1,\ldots,6\}, ℱd=2Ωd\mathcal F_d=2^{\Omega_d}, Pd(E)=|E|/6P_d(E)=|E|/6, and Z(ω)=ωZ(\omega)=\omega. Distinguish 44, {4}\{4\}, Z(4)Z(4) and Pd({4})P_d(\{4\}).

The outcome is 4; the singleton event is {4}\{4\}; the function value is Z(4)=4Z(4)=4; its probability is Pd({4})=1/6P_d(\{4\})=1/6. Also Z−1({2,4,6})={2,4,6}Z^{-1}(\{2,4,6\})=\{2,4,6\}, so Pd(Z is even)=1/2P_d(Z\text{ is even})=1/2.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
A continuous ticket-time question

Let TcT_c be the closure time, in hours, of a ticket from a specified process. Under an illustrative Gamma model with shape 2 and scale 12 hours, calculate P(Tc>24)P(T_c>24).

The model is stipulated for illustration, not estimated from the six-ticket audit. Its mean is αθ=2(12)=24\alpha\theta=2(12)=24 hours. The Gamma shape-scale density is f(t)=t144e−t/12f(t)=\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12} for t≥0t\ge0. The required probability is the area under this density to the right of 24 hours.

Read the units and parameterization aloud. Explain that shape 2 is not the mean; 24 hours is the mean under this shape-scale model.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
From counting to integration

For the six equally likely ticket IDs, an event probability is found by counting IDs. For continuous closure time under this density, what replaces counting individual durations?


For a ticket-ID event EE, P(E)=|E|/6P(E)=|E|/6. Under a continuous density model, probabilities are integrals over ranges. A density value is not itself a probability. The shaded right-tail area is P(Tc>24)=∫24∞t144e−t/12dtP(T_c>24)=\int_{24}^{\infty}\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12}\,dt.

Connect the shaded area to the integral, not to the height of the curve.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Evaluate the Gamma tail

Evaluate ∫24∞t144e−t/12dt\int_{24}^{\infty}\frac{t}{144}e^{-t/12}\,dt using u=t/12u=t/12. State the interpretation.

With u=t/12u=t/12, t=12ut=12u and dt=12dudt=12du: ∫2∞ue−udu=[−(u+1)e−u]2∞=3e−2≈0.406\int_2^\infty ue^{-u}du=[-(u+1)e^{-u}]_2^\infty=3e^{-2}\approx0.406. Under the stipulated model, about 0.406 of the probability lies above 24 hours.

Interpret only under the stated hypothetical model; do not present this as measured service-desk performance.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
What a density must satisfy

The stipulated closure-time density is f(t)=(t/144)e−t/12f(t)=(t/144)e^{-t/12} for t≥0t\ge0, and 0 otherwise. Does it integrate to one? What does a density specify?

∫0∞f(t)dt=∫0∞ue−udu=1\int_0^\infty f(t)dt=\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}du=1. A probability density is nonnegative and measurable, integrates to one, and satisfies P(T∈D)=∫Df(t)dtP(T\in D)=\int_D f(t)dt for Borel DD. A singleton has zero area: P(Tc=24)=0P(T_c=24)=0. The Billing indicator instead has a discrete law.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
The closure-time probability space

State the triplet for the closure-time calculation and define its random variable explicitly.

Ωc=[0,∞)\Omega_c=[0,\infty), ℱc=ℬ([0,∞))\mathcal F_c=\mathcal B([0,\infty)), and for E∈ℱcE\in\mathcal F_c, Pc(E)=∫E(t/144)e−t/12dtP_c(E)=\int_E (t/144)e^{-t/12}dt. Define Tc:Ωc→[0,∞)T_c:\Omega_c\to[0,\infty) by Tc(t)=tT_c(t)=t. Then Tc−1((24,∞))=(24,∞)T_c^{-1}((24,\infty))=(24,\infty) and Pc(Tc>24)=3e−2≈0.406P_c(T_c>24)=3e^{-2}\approx0.406. This is a canonical space modeling closure time alone.

Distinguish this triplet from the six-ticket ID triplet. In routine work, distribution notation often leaves the underlying space implicit.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Worked check: neither named destination

Under uniform selection from the six audited IDs, find the probability of “Other,” meaning neither Billing nor Account Support is required.

O=(B∪A)c={t4}O=(B\cup A)^c=\{t_4\}. Thus P(O)=1/6P(O)=1/6.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Worked check: exactly one destination

Find the event and probability that exactly one of Billing and Account Support is required.

(B\A)∪(A\B)={t2,t3,t5,t6}.(B\setminus A)\cup(A\setminus B)=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}.
Therefore its probability is 4/6=2/34/6=2/3.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Worked check: exact agreement

Let CC be the event that the model classification equals the reviewer reference outcome. Find CC and its probability in the uniform ticket-ID experiment.

C={t2,t3,t5,t6}C=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}, so P(C)=4/6=2/3P(C)=4/6=2/3. This equals the observed agreement fraction because the experiment selects one ticket ID uniformly from this exact six-ticket audit.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
section: Worked check: agreement as a random variable
text:
Worked check: agreement as a random variable

Define Y(t)=1Y(t)=1 for exact agreement and 0 otherwise. Find Y−1({1})Y^{-1}(\{1\}) and P(Y=1)P(Y=1).

Y−1({1})=C={t2,t3,t5,t6}Y^{-1}(\{1\})=C=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}. Thus P(Y=1)=P(C)=4/6=2/3P(Y=1)=P(C)=4/6=2/3. The random variable records an outcome numerically; its inverse image is the event; the measure assigns that event a number.

Give students time to set up the problem before discussing the result.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Weighted audit selection

Keep the six audit records, but select IDs with weights (1,1,1,3,1,1)/8(1,1,1,3,1,1)/8. Agreement is C={t2,t3,t5,t6}C=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}; Other is {t4}\{t_4\}. Find both probabilities.

The weights sum to one and define Q(E)=∑ti∈EwiQ(E)=\sum_{t_i\in E}w_i. Therefore Q(C)=4/8=1/2Q(C)=4/8=1/2 and Q(O)=3/8Q(O)=3/8. The observed fraction remains 4/64/6; the changed experiment gives a different selection probability.

Work the example, then connect it to the definition.
Reference: course 01.1 notes, §§1–8; rigorous supplement for formal derivations.

title: Probability through ticket triage
text:
Fraud-screen practice

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
What does a probability mean?

In a hypothetical agent benchmark, success was recorded on 90 of 100 tasks. What does the statement “success probability is 0.9” assert, and what does it assume?

The observed fraction is 0.9 on this benchmark. Treating it as a probability for future tasks requires a model connecting the benchmark tasks to the tasks of interest. The answer also depends on what probability is taken to mean: long-run frequency, coherent degree of belief, or a relation between evidence and a proposition. The axioms specify valid calculations; by themselves they do not select one interpretation.

The calculus and its interpretation

Separate two questions: which probability calculations are valid, and what do the numbers represent?

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Laplace’s classical rule

A fair die has six equally likely faces. What probability does the classical rule assign to an even face?

The classical rule is favourable cases divided by equally possible cases:
P(A)=number of favourable casesnumber of equally possible cases.P(A)=\frac{\text{number of favourable cases}}{\text{number of equally possible cases}}.
For a fair die, three of the six faces are even, so the rule gives 3/6=1/23/6=1/2. Hájek, §3.1, discusses Laplace’s formulation in the Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814).

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
The assumption behind counting

What justifies assigning the same probability to every face?

The classical rule needs an equally-likely partition. In the die example, fairness is the model assumption that gives each face probability 1/61/6. Counting then follows from that assumption. It does not establish fairness.

text:
A circular definition

Can “equally possible” define probability without already using a probability idea?

No. To call two cases equally possible is already to assert that neither has greater probability. The classical definition explains probability using a special case of probability. Keynes (1921) called the appeal to equal possibility the principle of indifference.

One experiment, two partitions

Toss a fair coin twice. What is the probability of at least one head? First list the ordered outcomes.

The ordered sample space is {HH,HT,TH,TT}\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}. Under independent fair tosses, each outcome has probability 1/41/4. The event is {HH,HT,TH}\{HH,HT,TH\}, so its probability is 3/43/4.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
section: The same event with three cases
text:
The same event with three cases

A three-case account lists: a head on the first toss; a tail then a head; two tails. Are these cases equally likely?

They form a disjoint, exhaustive partition: {HH,HT}\{HH,HT\}, {TH}\{TH\} and {TT}\{TT\}. Their probabilities are 1/21/2, 1/41/4 and 1/41/4. Only the first two cases include at least one head, so the probability is 1/2+1/4=3/41/2+1/4=3/4. Counting the cases as equal would give 2/32/3, which is incorrect for this partition.

Partition dependence

What failed in the three-case calculation?

The list itself is valid: exactly one case occurs. The error is assigning equal weights without justification. The same experiment admits different exhaustive partitions, and their parts need not have the same probabilities.

text:
When the counting rule is valid

State a condition under which P(A)=|A|/|Ω|P(A)=|A|/|\Omega| is justified for finite Ω\Omega.

If the model assigns equal probability to each of the finitely many outcomes, then each has probability 1/|Ω|1/|\Omega|. Finite additivity gives
P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω})=|A||Ω|.P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\})=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.
Thus counting is a consequence of the uniform finite model, not a definition that selects that model.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
section: A measured fraction is not a probability
text:
A measured fraction is not a probability

In nn observed trials, the event AA occurred Nn(A)N_n(A) times. What does Nn(A)/nN_n(A)/n describe?

It is the observed relative frequency:
fn(A)=Nn(A)n.f_n(A)=\frac{N_n(A)}{n}.
It is a statistic computed from a finite record. A probability belongs to a model. The two quantities are related in repeated-trial settings, but they are not the same definition.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
The frequency interpretation

How does the frequency account define the probability of AA?

It identifies probability with the limiting relative frequency of AA in an indefinitely long sequence of repetitions. Venn’s The Logic of Chance (1866) and von Mises’s work (1919; 1928) developed frequency accounts. Von Mises formulated them using infinite sequences called collectives.

Companion to Section 2 of the main notes. Source pointers appear on the final references slide.
Suggested discussion:

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
What is a collective?

Why did von Mises impose a condition on selected subsequences?

A collective is an infinite sequence in which relative frequencies of attributes converge and the limits remain unchanged under admissible selection rules that do not use the selected outcomes. If arbitrary selection were allowed, one could select subsequences based on outcomes and alter their frequencies. The admissible rules therefore need restriction; Church formalized place selection using recursive rules (see Hájek, §3.4).

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Limits of the frequency account

Can a finite run establish that the limiting relative frequency exists? What about a one-time event?

No finite record establishes an infinite limit. The frequency account postulates the limit rather than deriving it. It also requires an event to belong to a repeatable sequence, so it does not directly assign probability to a single non-repeatable event.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
A theorem or a definition?

Under the frequency interpretation, is convergence a theorem? Under the axioms, what is its status?

Under the frequency definition, convergence is true by construction. Under the axioms, convergence is a theorem under stated hypotheses. For independent, identically distributed Bernoulli trials with success probability pp, the strong law gives convergence of the observed success frequency to pp with probability one. A theorem makes its hypotheses explicit.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Probability as degree of belief

How might a probability describe uncertainty about an event that will not be repeated?

Subjective accounts interpret probability as a degree of belief. Ramsey (1926) and de Finetti (1931, 1937) connected a person’s probability for AA to betting quotients they would accept. This approach can address one-off events as well as repeated trials.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Coherence constrains beliefs

What condition prevents a system of betting probabilities from guaranteeing a loss?

Coherence requires that the assigned betting quotients do not permit a set of bets that loses in every outcome. This requirement forces finite addition rules. The calculus is recovered from a consistency condition on the degrees of belief.

text:
Finite and countable additivity

Does coherence alone justify countable additivity?

De Finetti argued that this reasoning justifies finite additivity, not countable additivity. That is a mathematical difference from Kolmogorov’s third axiom. Several standard limit theorems fail without countable additivity.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
section: Probability as a relation to evidence
text:
Probability as a relation to evidence

Can probability be understood as a relation between evidence and a proposition, rather than a personal belief?

Logical accounts treat probability as partial entailment: a relation between evidence and a proposition that is not defined by an individual’s opinion. Keynes (1921), Jeffreys (1939) and Carnap (1950) developed versions of this programme. It seeks a canonical assignment when evidence is incomplete.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
The principle of indifference returns

How does the logical account face the difficulty of assigning probabilities without enough evidence?

It may appeal to a canonical assignment or the principle of indifference. But indifference depends on how possibilities are partitioned. The two-toss example showed that exhaustive cases need not be equally probable. The logical account therefore faces the same partition-dependence as the classical rule.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Fiducial probability

What was Fisher’s fiducial argument intended to obtain?

Fisher (1930) proposed deriving probability statements about an unknown parameter from its sampling distribution, without assuming a prior distribution. The aim was to obtain interval statements in applied statistics without the subjective element of a prior.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
section: What fiducial probability is—and is not
text:
What fiducial probability is—and is not

Is fiducial probability an alternative interpretation of the probability calculus?

It concerns inferential statements about unknown parameters; it is not an account of what probability means generally. It is therefore not an alternative to the axioms in the same sense as frequency or degree-of-belief accounts. Fisher’s 1930 proposal is nearly contemporary with Kolmogorov’s 1933 axiomatization. Parameter-distribution methods need their own assumptions; a sampling distribution alone does not automatically supply a unique probability law for an unknown parameter. See Reid, slides 7–8 and 16.

section: Bertrand: a question without a sampling rule
text:
Bertrand: a question without a sampling rule

If someone says “choose a chord at random,” is the probability model specified?

No. The phrase does not identify a probability measure on the chord space. Bertrand’s paradox shows that different defensible sampling mechanisms give different probabilities for the same geometric event. Specify the mechanism—for example, what quantity is uniform—and the model is well posed. This diagnosis needs no new mathematics.

text:
What Bertrand does not explain

Does specifying a sampling rule provide a framework for proving results about infinite sequences or processes?

No. Bertrand illustrates the need to specify the model, but it does not provide the mathematical language for infinite sequences, continuous-time processes, or conditioning on null events. Those require probability measures on suitable spaces and events.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Measure theory preceded the axioms

Was measure theory invented to resolve Bertrand’s paradox?

No. Measure and integration supply a way to assign mass to sets and calculate probabilities on infinite outcome spaces. Measure theory supplied tools for formulating and proving probability results beyond finite counting.

Infinite sequences need measurable events

To say that relative frequencies converge with probability one, what set must be an event?

The set of infinite outcome sequences on which the frequencies converge must belong to the event σ-algebra. Countable additivity and closure under countable unions support such statements. Finite additivity alone is insufficient for the standard limit theory.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Processes on function spaces

What kind of probability space can represent a random continuous path?

A process such as Brownian motion can be represented by a probability measure on a space of continuous functions. Kolmogorov’s extension theorem gives conditions under which consistent finite-dimensional distributions determine a measure on an infinite product space.

title: Probability before Kolmogorov
text:
Conditioning on a probability-zero event

Why does P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)/P(B)P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B) not define conditioning when P(B)=0P(B)=0?

The denominator is zero. In continuous models, exact-value events commonly have probability zero, so the elementary ratio cannot define conditional probabilities there. Kolmogorov’s conditional expectation relative to a σ-algebra supplies a more general object, defined up to events of probability zero. Specifying a value on an individual null event requires additional structure; the elementary ratio alone is insufficient.

A shared mathematical framework

What do finite audits, continuous measurements and random paths need in common?

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Chord length from the midpoint distance
text:
Chord length from the midpoint distance

Let D be the distance from the centre to the chord. Express its length L in terms of D.


The right triangle gives (L/2)2+D2=R2(L/2)^2+D^2=R^2.
Therefore L=2R2−D2L=2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Converting the long-chord condition

Using L=2R2−D2L=2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}, express the strict condition L>3RL>\sqrt3R as an inequality for DD.

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving
(L/2)2+D2=R2,L=2R2−D2.(L/2)^2+D^2=R^2,\qquad L=2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}.
Now apply the strict threshold:
2R2−D2>3R.2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}>\sqrt3R.
Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring is valid:
4(R2−D2)>3R2⇔D2<R2/4.4(R^2-D^2)>3R^2\iff D^2<R^2/4.
Since D≥0D\ge0, the event is D<R/2D<R/2.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
A numerical geometry check

For R=10R=10 cm and L=2R2−D2L=2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}, calculate LL when D=3D=3 cm and when D=6D=6 cm. Compare both lengths with 3R\sqrt3R.

At D=3D=3 cm: L=2100−9=291≈19.08L=2\sqrt{100-9}=2\sqrt{91}\approx19.08 cm.
At D=6D=6 cm: L=2100−36=16L=2\sqrt{100-36}=16 cm.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Experiment I: a uniform angle at a fixed endpoint
text:
Experiment I: a uniform angle at a fixed endpoint

Use a unit circle and fix a=(1,0)a=(1,0). Choose θ\theta uniformly in (0,π)(0,\pi), measured from the upward tangent towards the disk. Find the long-chord probability.

The resulting chord has length L=2sin⁡θL=2\sin\,\theta.
L>3⇔π/3<θ<2π/3.L>\sqrt3\iff\pi/3<\theta<2\pi/3.
The favorable interval occupies one third of the angular range:
2π/3−π/3π=13.\frac{2\pi/3-\pi/3}{\pi}=\frac13.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Experiment II: a uniform distance

Choose rr uniformly in (0,1)(0,1). Set the midpoint to (r,0)(r,0) and draw the vertical chord through it. Find the long-chord probability.

L=21−r2,L>3⇔r<1/2.L=2\sqrt{1-r^2},\qquad L>\sqrt3\iff r<1/2.
Half the available distance interval is favorable:
1/21=12.\frac{1/2}{1}=\frac12.
Fixing the midpoint direction specifies which chord is drawn.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Experiment III: a uniform midpoint

Choose a midpoint uniformly by area in the unit disk. Draw the chord perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the long-chord probability.

The midpoint must lie inside the concentric disk of radius 1/21/2.
π(1/2)2π=14.\frac{\pi(1/2)^2}{\pi}=\frac14.
The centre and boundary have area zero; omit them to make the construction unique and nondegenerate.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: The angle experiment as a triplet
text:
The angle experiment as a triplet
Ω1=(0,π),ℱ1=ℬ((0,π)).\Omega_1=(0,\pi),\qquad\mathcal F_1=\mathcal B((0,\pi)).
For a Borel event BB, define
P1(B)=1π∫Bdθ.P_1(B)=\frac1\pi\int_B d\theta.
E1=(π/3,2π/3),P1(E1)=13.E_1=(\pi/3,2\pi/3),\qquad P_1(E_1)=\frac13.
ℬ\mathcal B denotes the Borel σ-algebra generated by the open sets.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: The distance experiment as a triplet
text:
The distance experiment as a triplet
Ω2=(0,1),ℱ2=ℬ((0,1)).\Omega_2=(0,1),\qquad\mathcal F_2=\mathcal B((0,1)).
For a Borel event BB, define
P2(B)=∫Bdr.P_2(B)=\int_B dr.
E2=(0,1/2),P2(E2)=12.E_2=(0,1/2),\qquad P_2(E_2)=\frac12.
The fixed midpoint direction is part of the construction.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: The midpoint experiment as a triplet
text:
The midpoint experiment as a triplet
D*={(x,y):0<x2+y2<1}.D^*=\{(x,y):0<x^2+y^2<1\}.
Ω3=D*,ℱ3=ℬ(D*).\Omega_3=D^*,\qquad\mathcal F_3=\mathcal B(D^*).
P3(B)=1π∬Bdxdy.P_3(B)=\frac1\pi\iint_B dx\,dy.

The omitted centre and boundary have area zero.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: The probability triplets resolve the contradiction
text:
The probability triplets resolve the contradiction
With the probability triplets specified, the apparent contradiction is resolved: the three answers belong to three different probability models.
P1(E1)=13,P2(E2)=12,P3(E3)=14.P_1(E_1)=\frac13,\qquad P_2(E_2)=\frac12,\qquad P_3(E_3)=\frac14.
Stopping point. The resolution is complete. The remaining slides study sampling maps and induced measures on a common chord space.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Exercise: connect the constructions

Randomize the first endpoint in Experiment I uniformly, independently of θ\theta. Show that this gives two independent uniform endpoints.
Give Experiment II an independent uniform midpoint direction. Does its length distribution change?
Explain why an equal length distribution need not mean an equal measure on chords.

Exercise 8 in the supplement states the full problem.
In the advanced section, Model A uses independent uniform endpoints; B uses independent uniform distance and direction; C uses uniform midpoint area.

text:

Let t=D/Rt=D/R and let ϕ\phi be the direction of the midpoint from the centre.
Place the midpoint at distance RtRt in direction ϕ\phi, then draw the perpendicular chord.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Recovering the chord coordinates

For midpoint mm and radius RR, define t=∥m∥/Rt=\|m\|/R and ϕ=Arg⁡(m)∈[0,2π)\phi=\operatorname{Arg}(m)\in[0,2\pi). Recover (ϕ,t)(\phi,t) from the chord.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Model B: uniform radial distance

Sample DD uniformly on (0,R)(0,R) and independently ϕ\phi uniformly on [0,2π)[0,2\pi). For L=2R2−D2L=2\sqrt{R^2-D^2}, find the probability of L>3RL>\sqrt3R.

The event is D<R/2D<R/2.
The favourable radial interval has length R/2R/2, out of total length RR:
PB(L>3R)=R/2R=12.P_B(L>\sqrt3R)=\frac{R/2}{R}=\frac12.
This model is uniform in radial distance.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Model B: sampling map and inverse
text:
Model B: sampling map and inverse

Let U,VU,V be independent uniforms on (0,1)(0,1) and [0,1)[0,1), and set t=Ut=U, ϕ=2πV\phi=2\pi V. Using C(ϕ,t)C(\phi,t), write the chord, recover (U,V)(U,V), and express its length.

t=U,ϕ=2πV,c=C(2πV,U).t=U,\qquad \phi=2\pi V,\qquad c=C(2\pi V,U).
From the sampled chord, recover
U=t,V=ϕ/(2π).U=t,\qquad V=\phi/(2\pi).

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Model C: a midpoint uniform in disk area
text:
Model C: a midpoint uniform in disk area

Choose the chord midpoint uniformly by area in a disk of radius R. The long-chord event is D<R/2. Find the probability.

Long chords have midpoints within radius R/2R/2.
Uniform area sampling gives
PC(L>3R)=π(R/2)2πR2=14.P_C(L>\sqrt3R)=\frac{\pi(R/2)^2}{\pi R^2}=\frac14.
The smaller disk occupies a quarter of the total area.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Why uniform area uses a square root
text:
Why uniform area uses a square root

For a midpoint sampled uniformly by area in a radius-R disk and U uniform on (0,1), derive P(D<r) and the corresponding transformation of U.

P(D<r)=πr2πR2=(rR)2.P(D<r)=\frac{\pi r^2}{\pi R^2}=\left(\frac rR\right)^2.
The transformation D=RUD=R\sqrt U has exactly this property:
P(RU<r)=P(U<(r/R)2)=(r/R)2.P(R\sqrt U<r)=P\!\left(U<(r/R)^2\right)=(r/R)^2.
Using D=RUD=RU instead would give uniform radial distance.

Reference: Jagannathan, Chapter 4; rigorous supplement §3 for the sampling maps and derivations.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Model C: sampling map and inverse
text:
Model C: sampling map and inverse

For uniform disk area, set t=Ut=\sqrt U, ϕ=2πV\phi=2\pi V, with independent uniforms U,VU,V on (0,1)(0,1) and [0,1)[0,1). Using C(ϕ,t)C(\phi,t), write the chord, its inverse and its length.

t=U,ϕ=2πV,c=C(2πV,U).t=\sqrt U,\qquad \phi=2\pi V,\qquad c=C(2\pi V,\sqrt U).
Inverse: U=t2U=t^2, V=ϕ/(2π)V=\phi/(2\pi).
The length is LC=2R1−UL_C=2R\sqrt{1-U}.
The long-chord event is U<1/4U<1/4, which has probability 1/41/4.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Practice: a smaller midpoint region

For the same disk of radius R, find P(D<R/3) under (i) a uniform radial distance and (ii) a midpoint chosen uniformly by disk area.

Model B, uniform radial distance:
PB(D<R/3)=R/3R=13.P_B(D<R/3)=\frac{R/3}{R}=\frac13.

title: Bertrand’s paradox
section: Changing coordinates in one fixed model
text:

Keep Model B, where T=D/RT=D/R is uniform on (0,1)(0,1). Put W=T2W=T^2. What is P(W<1/4)P(W<1/4)?
